source: Common personal-finance advice as it circulates — the 4% rule, 'never touch the emergency fund', 'always take the match', 'pay yourself first', 'save 10%', 'a house is an investment', 'rent is throwing money away', 'cut the coffee' — each restated for one household's numbers. The rules of thumb are conventions; the translations are arithmetic on the household's own figures.
confidenceNote: None of these is a finding. Each is a piece of advice people hear, marked learn (worth taking, and here is what it means for you) or unlearn (worth dropping, and here is why for you). The order is a judgement about what usually matters first.
note: Each item: `when` names predicates engines/advice.js evaluates against the household (all must hold); `priority` orders ties (lower first); `body` carries {tokens} the engine fills. `room`/`anchor` say where to act. D-096.

items.headline: “Never touch your emergency fund.”
items.body: This is what it is for. {cash} of cash covers {cashMonths} of your {spending} a month; drawing on it now is the fund working, not failing.

items.headline: “Always take the whole match.”
items.body: For you that is {matchGap} a year you are not collecting — a raise your employer already agreed to. Raising your contribution to {matchCap} takes it.

items.headline: “The 4% rule.”
items.body: You draw {withdrawalRate} of your investments a year to cover what income does not — {annualDraw}. Under 4% the convention says the money outlasts you; above 5% it starts to worry.

items.headline: “Retirement means living off the portfolio.”
items.body: What comes in, {income} a month, covers your {spending} a month, so nothing is drawn. The {investments} invested is a reserve of {investmentYears} of spending, not a paycheque — and the 4% rule has nothing to say until it is.

items.headline: “Pay yourself first.”
items.body: Your savings rate is {savingsRate}; the floor most guidance uses is {floor}. For you the gap is {gapMonthly} a month, moved before the month starts rather than found at its end.

items.headline: “Pay off high-interest debt before investing.”
items.body: {highInterestBalance} of what you owe charges more than most markets return. Every dollar at it earns that rate, guaranteed, which no fund promises.

items.headline: “Student loans follow you forever.”
items.body: At the minimums yours clear in {loanYear}. Every extra {hundred} a month moves that earlier; the payoff room shows by how much.

items.headline: “Set aside a third for tax.”
items.body: On {gross} a year the estimate is {tax}, {effectiveRate} — about {taxMonthly} a month put somewhere it cannot be spent, and a quarterly to pay.

items.headline: “Save 10% and you are fine.”
items.body: You are at {savingsRate}, already past it, and the number that matters now is not the rate but the date it points to: {fiYear}. The rate is a lever on the date, not a finish line.

items.headline: “Cut the coffee.”
items.body: At your real hourly wage of {wage} a {coffee} coffee is {coffeeTime} of your life; your rent is {rentTime}. Pointing at the small one is the mistake.

items.headline: “Three to six months of expenses in cash.”
items.body: You hold {cashMonths} of your {spending} a month. Three months is {threeMonths}; you are {cashGap} short of that floor.

items.headline: “Rent is throwing money away.”
items.body: Rent buys a place to live, the way a mortgage's interest, tax, insurance and upkeep do — none of which build equity either. The question is the price-to-rent ratio where you are, not the word.

items.headline: “Cash is safe.”
items.body: You hold {cashMonths} of spending in cash. Past six months the excess — {cashExcess} — loses to inflation every year it sits; the runway does not need it.

items.headline: “It is never too early, or too late.”
items.body: The first number to know is what a month costs you: {spending}. Every other number on this page is measured against it.
